Reconstruct rounding bounds

Source: R/unround.R
unround.Rd

unround() takes a rounded number and returns the range of values that would have been rounded to it: a lower and an upper bound, and whether each is inclusive. The default rounding method is "up_or_down"; see Rounding for the others.

Usage

unround(
  x,
  rounding = "up_or_down",
  threshold = 5,
  digits = NULL,
  symmetric = FALSE
)

Arguments

x

String or numeric. The rounded number. Must be a string unless digits is specified. A missing or infinite x has NA bounds.

rounding

String. The rounding method assumed to have produced x. Default is "up_or_down". See Rounding.

threshold

Numeric. For the "*_from" methods, the point within a step at which rounding switches direction, in tenths of a step; greater than 0 and less than 10. Default is 5. See round_up_from().

digits

Integer. The number of decimal places in x. Default is NULL, in which case it is counted from the string x. Specify it if the number is already known, as a function that uses unround() as a helper would.

symmetric

Logical. If TRUE, negative numbers are assumed to have been rounded like their absolute values under "up", "down", and the "*_from" methods. Default is FALSE. Must not be TRUE with a "ties_*" method; see reround().

Value

A tibble with the columns range, rounding, lower, incl_lower, x, incl_upper, and upper. range summarizes the columns from lower to upper.

Details

x is a string by default so that its trailing zeros can be counted, since a numeric value loses them. If the number of decimal places is known, pass it as digits, and x may be numeric. bound_numerators() and sum_range() derive their bounds from the same internal functions as unround(), so they always agree with it.

All arguments are vectorized. Those of length greater than 1 must have the same length and are paired element by element. Pairing x with rounding in this way gives a warning.

Rounding

Whether a bound is inclusive depends on the rounding method. Under "up", a value on the lower bound rounds up to x, but a value on the upper bound rounds up past it. The range column shows the bounds with the appropriate signs:

Value of roundingCorresponding range
"up_or_down" (default)lower <= x <= upper
"up", "ties_up"lower <= x < upper
"down", "ties_down"lower < x <= upper
"ties_away" (positive x)lower <= x < upper
"ties_away" (negative x)lower < x <= upper
"ties_zero" (positive x)lower < x <= upper
"ties_zero" (negative x)lower <= x < upper
"ties_away", "ties_zero" (zero x)lower < x < upper
"even", "ties_even"lower <= x <= upper
"ceiling"lower < x = upper
"floor"lower = x < upper
"ceiling_or_floor"lower < x < upper
"trunc" (positive x)lower = x < upper
"trunc" (negative x)lower < x = upper
"trunc" (zero x)lower < x < upper
"anti_trunc" (positive x)lower < x = upper
"anti_trunc" (negative x)lower = x < upper
"anti_trunc" (zero x)lower = x = upper (all 0)
"up_from"lower <= x < upper
"down_from"lower < x <= upper
"up_from_or_down_from"lower <= x <= upper

threshold only applies to the three "*_from" methods. It moves their range without widening it; each spans exactly one step at every threshold.

The "ties_*" methods each name a complete tie-breaking procedure, so giving symmetric = TRUE with them is an error; see round_ties_up().

Under "even", both bounds are reported as inclusive. base::round() decides a tie on the binary double, so whether a value on a bound rounds to x cannot be predicted from its decimal digits. Treating both bounds as inclusive can only widen the range, which is the safe direction for error detection.

See also

round_up() for rounding up or down from 5, and round_ceiling() for the one-directional methods.

Examples

# By default, `x` may have been rounded up or down:
unround(x = "2.7")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   range                  rounding   lower incl_lower x     incl_upper upper
#>   <chr>                  <chr>      <dbl> <lgl>      <chr> <lgl>      <dbl>
#> 1 2.65 <= x(2.7) <= 2.75 up_or_down  2.65 TRUE       2.7   TRUE        2.75

# If it was rounded up, the upper bound is exclusive:
unround(x = "2.7", rounding = "up")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   range                 rounding lower incl_lower x     incl_upper upper
#>   <chr>                 <chr>    <dbl> <lgl>      <chr> <lgl>      <dbl>
#> 1 2.65 <= x(2.7) < 2.75 up        2.65 TRUE       2.7   FALSE       2.75

# Likewise with rounding down...
unround(x = "2.7", rounding = "down")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   range                 rounding lower incl_lower x     incl_upper upper
#>   <chr>                 <chr>    <dbl> <lgl>      <chr> <lgl>      <dbl>
#> 1 2.65 < x(2.7) <= 2.75 down      2.65 FALSE      2.7   TRUE        2.75

# ...and with `base::round()`:
unround(x = "2.7", rounding = "even")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   range                  rounding lower incl_lower x     incl_upper upper
#>   <chr>                  <chr>    <dbl> <lgl>      <chr> <lgl>      <dbl>
#> 1 2.65 <= x(2.7) <= 2.75 even      2.65 TRUE       2.7   TRUE        2.75

# One row per input value:
unround(x = c(3.6, "5.20", 5.174))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 7
#>   range                        rounding  lower incl_lower x     incl_upper upper
#>   <chr>                        <chr>     <dbl> <lgl>      <chr> <lgl>      <dbl>
#> 1 3.55 <= x(3.6) <= 3.65       up_or_do…  3.55 TRUE       3.6   TRUE        3.65
#> 2 5.195 <= x(5.20) <= 5.205    up_or_do…  5.20 TRUE       5.20  TRUE        5.20
#> 3 5.1735 <= x(5.174) <= 5.1745 up_or_do…  5.17 TRUE       5.174 TRUE        5.17
